newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian govt wins on retirement savings plan.
newsitem.headline: Australian govt wins on retirement savings plan.

text.p: The Australian government had pushed its retirement savings account legislation through the upper house of parliament, the Senate, with only a few minor changes, a government spokesman said on Tuesday.

A spokesman for Assistant Treasurer Rod Kemp said the government had agreed to a number of amendments proposed by the Australian Democrats minor party in order to secure the bill's passage through the Senate, after it was blocked there in March.
"When I say they were minor, some of them we weren't happy with but we simply passed to ensure that the bill did get through," the spokesman told Reuters.
"So there was that balance where we had to compromise on a few, whereas in a perfect world we would have liked not to have some of them."

Under the legislation, banks and insurance companies will be able to offer Retirement Savings Accounts (RSAs) as an alternative to superannuation (pensions) for low-income and itinerant workers and for workers with more than one job.
-- a guarantee all regulations aim to ensure RSAs are low cost;
-- a freedom of choice clause, which meant that employers must provide employees with three or four alternative retirement saving options;
-- a liability clause preventing a provider from acting improperly in offering RSAs; and

-- the removal of the due diligence defence, meaning an employee could take action against the provider for misleading information even if the provider had relied on another party for that information.
The spokesman said the government had supported the last amendment purely to ensure the passage of the bill, which was passed with the support of the Democrats late on Monday night.
The government needs two non-government votes to pass any legislation in the Senate, where it does not hold a clear majority.
The Opposition and the Democrats both voted against the bill in March, saying the proposed accounts' rate of return would be significantly lower than that of the superannuation funds.
